headline: Council unanimously approves Franklin Street redesign plan, moving project to next design phase.
summary: Along the corridor, the plan adds 1.5 miles of sidewalks and separated bike lanes from Marginal Way to Commercial Street. The planning director estimates 530 to 720 new housing units on more than 3.5 acres of new land. The next phase, preliminary design, is already funded by a federal grant, impact fees, and a state match. Separately, the council recommended a tariff change to prohibit scrubber discharge at city-owned marine terminals.
decisions: Approved appointing Philip crew us as a constable for the Portland Police Department, passed unanimously.
Approved three consent-calendar liquor license orders, including one for 1050 Westbrook Brook Street.
Approved the Reimagining Franklin Street Plan and planning study, passed unanimously.
Failed on a 4-4 tie: amendment asking the city manager to seek scrubber discharge records from commercial vessels.
Recommended a tariff change to prohibit scrubber discharge at city-owned marine terminals, unanimously, 8 in favor.
Approved accepting and appropriating an additional $74,572.50 from the Land and Water Conservation Fund for Riverton Trolley Park, passed unanimously.
Approved amendment to the conditional zoning agreement for property near St. Loris Arts on Congress Street, reducing the proposal to a single 424-seat auditorium, by roll call.
Approved accepting and appropriating $20,000 in Maine Emergency Management Agency grants for fire department hazmat training, passed as an emergency.
Approved modification to the Maine Department of Transportation project agreement for bike and pedestrian safety on West Commercial Street, passed as an emergency.
discussion: Franklin Street tree removal: Public speakers praised the plan but objected to clearing trees along the corridor, and said saplings take 20 to 50 years to match mature trees. Council members asked for a study of tree loss, a memo on how many trees can be moved, and more public engagement in the next phase.

Portland Housing Authority conditions: Public speakers described roach and bed bug infestations at a Boyd Street building and asked for accountability. Council remarks said the housing authority is quasi-independent and that complaints can go to the HUD office in Boston.

Scrubber discharge ban: Public speakers backed the ban, and the Portland Regional Chamber asked for clear compliance steps, since Portland does not yet have shore power. The parks and facilities director said no ships booked for 2027 appear affected, and the corporation counsel said a federal rule may later preempt the local tariff.

Metro 2027 transit budget: Metro's executive director presented a $23.5 million budget, about 14% higher than 2026. The director said Portland's assessment would rise about 15%, or $539,000, to about $4.1 million, mainly because one-time funding ended.
